mad1-w1-q1.question: A browser opens this URL: `https://shop.example.com:8443/items/list?page=2&sort=price#reviews`. Which part of the URL is **not** sent to the server with the HTTP request?
options: The host `shop.example.com` (which goes in the `Host` header)
mad1-w1-q1.explanation: The fragment (the part after `#`) is only for the browser, for example to scroll to a section of the page; the browser does not include it in the request. The path and query go in the request line (`GET /items/list?page=2&sort=price HTTP/1.1`) and the host goes in the `Host` header, so options A, C and D are wrong. Trap: option A, because people think the query is also browser-only, while the server uses it to filter and sort.

mad1-w1-q2.question: In an app, the `/login` route accepts only GET and POST. A client sends a `DELETE /login` request. Which status code is the most accurate?
mad1-w1-q2.explanation: The resource (`/login`) exists; this method just isn't allowed on it. That is 405, and the response's `Allow` header lists the allowed methods (GET, POST). Option A's trap: the resource was found, so 404 is wrong. Option D (501) is for a server that doesn't recognise the method for any resource at all. Option B (403) is about missing permission, not about the method.

mad1-w1-q3.question: A 2 MB file is downloaded over a 16 Mbps link with an RTT of 80 ms. Before data arrives, 2 RTTs are needed (TCP handshake + request); ignore TLS and server time. 1 MB = 10⁶ bytes, 1 Mbps = 10⁶ bits/s. What is the total time?
mad1-w1-q3.explanation: Latency: 2 × 80 ms = 0.16 s. Transmission: 2 MB = 16 × 10⁶ bits, and 16 × 10⁶ ÷ 16 × 10⁶ = 1.0 s. Total = 0.16 + 1.0 = 1.16 s. Option A's trap: not converting bytes to bits (2 ÷ 16 = 0.125 s, plus 0.16). Option B forgets the latency, and option C counts only 1 RTT.

mad1-w1-q4.question: A browser sends `GET /old-page` and the server replies `301 Moved Permanently` with the header `Location: /new-page`. What happens next?
options: The browser automatically sends a new GET request for `/new-page`, and the address bar shows `/new-page`
The server fetches the content of `/new-page` internally and sends it in the body of that same 301 response
The browser shows the user an error page, because 3xx codes are failures
The browser waits a little and requests `/old-page` again
mad1-w1-q4.explanation: A 3xx redirect means 'the resource is elsewhere': the browser reads the `Location` header and sends a **new request** there, so there are two request-response cycles and the URL changes. Option B's trap: that is like a server-side forward/include, not a redirect; in a redirect the client does the work. Option C is wrong because 3xx is not an error class, and option D is thinking of `Retry-After`/503.

mad1-w1-q5.question: In a fresh browser (no caches) a user opens `https://www.example.org/`. The connection is HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 over TCP. Which order is correct?
options: TCP handshake → DNS lookup → TLS handshake → HTTP request
DNS lookup → TCP handshake → TLS handshake → HTTP request
DNS lookup → TLS handshake → TCP handshake → HTTP request
HTTP request → DNS lookup → TCP handshake → TLS handshake
mad1-w1-q5.explanation: A TCP connection needs an IP address, so DNS comes first. TLS runs on top of TCP, so the TLS handshake comes after TCP. Only once the encrypted channel exists does the HTTP request go out. Option C's trap: putting TLS before TCP because 'security comes first'; but TLS needs a TCP connection to send its bytes. Option A starts TCP without an IP, which isn't possible.

mad1-w1-q6.question: Plain HTTP/1.1 (no TLS), DNS already cached, RTT 50 ms. A browser loads an HTML page that references 5 more files (3 CSS/JS + 2 images, same server). No TCP connection is open yet; the browser opens one **persistent** TCP connection and requests the files one after another (no pipelining). Ignore transmission and server time. What is the minimum time to get all 6 files?
mad1-w1-q6.explanation: TCP handshake = 1 RTT. Then the HTML request-response = 1 RTT, and the other 5 files one after another = 5 RTTs. Total 7 RTTs × 50 ms = 350 ms. Option A's trap: that is the non-persistent connection count, where every file needs a new handshake (6 × 2 × 50 = 600 ms). Option D forgets the handshake (6 × 50), and option B assumes all the files arrived at once.

mad1-w2-q1.question: Which markup is the most accessible for an email input, so that clicking the label focuses the input and a screen reader announces the field's name?
options: `<label>Email</label> <input type="email" name="email">` (label outside the input, no `for`)
mad1-w2-q1.explanation: The label's `for` matches the input's `id`, so the label is programmatically tied to that input: a click focuses it and a screen reader announces the field as 'Email'. Option A's trap: a placeholder disappears as soon as you type and does not replace a label. Option C has a `<label>`, but with no `for` and the input not inside it there is no link; option B's `<span>` is just text.

mad1-w2-q2.question: In this CSS `box-sizing` is not set anywhere (default). What is the card's visible width (from one edge of the border to the other)?
mad1-w2-q2.explanation: With the default `content-box`, `width` is only the content: 300 + 2 × 20 (padding) + 2 × 5 (border) = 350px. Option A's trap: thinking like `border-box`, where 300px would include everything. Option B forgets the border, and option D also adds the margin, but the margin is empty space outside the border, not part of the visible box.

mad1-w2-q3.question: The user presses Go without changing anything. Which URL will the browser request?
options: `/search` (the data goes in the request body)
mad1-w2-q3.explanation: Only controls with a `name` are submitted: `q=flask` and the select's `sort`. A select's value is the chosen option's `value` attribute (`new`), not its visible text (`Newest`). Option B's trap: the `lang` input has only an `id`, no `name`, so it isn't sent. Option C sends the display text, and option D is POST behaviour, while the method here is GET.

mad1-w2-q4.question:
The HTML is `
Home
` and the CSS is below. What colour is the "Home" link?
options: the browser's default link colour, because the rules conflict
mad1-w2-q4.explanation: Specificity: `#menu a` = (1, 0, 1), `nav a.active` = (0, 1, 2), `.link.active` = (0, 2, 0). The comparison goes from the left and only the first rule has an id, so red wins. Option A's trap: 'the last rule wins' or 'two classes are more'; source order only matters when specificity is equal. Option D is wrong because the cascade always resolves a conflict.

mad1-w2-q5.question: The viewport width is first 768px, then 400px. What is the width of `.col` in each case?
mad1-w2-q5.explanation: `max-width: 768px` means width ≤ 768px, so at 768px the first query applies and the width is 100%. At 400px both queries match; specificity is equal, so the later rule (90%) wins. Option A's trap: reading `max-width` as 'strictly less than'. Option B's trap: thinking that after the first matching media query the rest are ignored; in CSS every matching rule enters the cascade.

mad1-w2-q6.question: Two `<div>`s sit one below the other in normal block flow (the parent is a plain block, not flex/grid), with no padding, border or content between them. What is the vertical gap between the border of "One" and the border of "Two"?
mad1-w2-q6.explanation: In normal flow the vertical margins of adjacent block siblings **collapse**: the gap is the larger of the two margins, i.e. max(30, 20) = 30px. Option A's trap: adding the margins as you would horizontally (30 + 20). Collapsing happens only for vertical margins in block flow; margins of flex or grid items don't collapse, and there you would get 50px. Option D's 10px is the difference, which no rule uses.

mad1-w3-q1.question: The context has `courses = ['MAD1', 'DBMS']`. What does this (one-line) template render?
mad1-w3-q1.explanation: In Jinja `loop.index` starts at 1 and goes up on every iteration, so you get `1.MAD1 2.DBMS`. Option B's trap: counting from 0 like Python's `enumerate`; that would be `loop.index0`. Option D assumes the index never increases, and option C has the order reversed.

mad1-w3-q2.question:
A Flask app renders `

{{ comment }}

` in a `comment.html` template, and a user wrote `hi` as the comment. With default settings, what does the browser show?
options: The literal text `hi`, because `<` and `>` were escaped to `<` and `>`
The template fails to render with an error
The `<b>` tags are removed and only a plain 'hi' is shown
mad1-w3-q2.explanation: Flask turns autoescaping on for `.html` templates, so the special characters in `{{ comment }}` become HTML entities and the browser shows them as text, not as tags. Option A's trap: that only happens with `|safe` (and then a `<script>` would run too). Option D is 'sanitizing', which autoescaping does not do; it doesn't strip tags, it turns them into harmless text.

mad1-w3-q3.question: The template is the same both times. First `user = {'name': 'Asha'}` (no `nickname` key) is passed, then `user = {'name': 'Asha', 'nickname': ''}`. What are the two outputs?
options: An error the first time, `Hi !` the second time
mad1-w3-q3.explanation: The first time there is no `nickname` key, so `user.nickname` is undefined and `default` gives 'Guest'. The second time the key exists and its value is an empty string; `default` only acts on undefined values, so the empty string is printed: `Hi !`. Option A's trap: treating `default` like Python's `or`; for that you need `default('Guest', true)`. Option C is wrong because with default settings a missing key does not raise an error.

mad1-w3-q4.question: `base.html` has `<title>{% block title %}Site{% endblock %}</title>`. When the `profile.html` below is rendered, what is the title, and does "Hello" appear on the page?
options: `<title>Profile - Site</title>`, and "Hello" also appears on the page
`<title>Site</title>`, because a parent's block cannot be overridden
mad1-w3-q4.explanation: The child's `title` block replaces the parent's block, and `{{ super() }}` brings back the parent's content 'Site', so the title is `Profile - Site`. In a template that extends another, text outside blocks (here "Hello") is not rendered, because the output is the parent's layout. Option A's trap: treating the child like a normal page where everything is printed. Option B ignores `super()`, and option D gets the meaning of block overriding backwards.

mad1-w3-q5.question: The header has a link ``; there is no text in the link, only a cart icon. What is the best `alt` for the image?
mad1-w3-q5.explanation: Here the image is the link's entire content, so its `alt` becomes the link's accessible name. So the alt should state what the link does: 'View cart'. Option B's trap: `alt=""` is for decorative images that already have text next to them; here it would leave the link without a name and a screen reader would just say 'link'. Option C makes it read a filename that is useless to users, and in option D `title` is not a reliable replacement.

mad1-w3-q6.question: The context has `nums = [3, 4, 7, 8, 10]`. What does this (one-line) template render?
mad1-w3-q6.explanation: `for ... if ...` filters the sequence first, and the `loop` variable counts only the items that enter the loop: 4, 8, 10 get indices 1, 2, 3. Option A's trap: that is what happens with an `{% if %}` inside the loop, where `loop.index` counts positions in the original list (including 3). Option B is like `loop.index0`, and option C reads the condition backwards (odd numbers).

mad1-w4-q1.question: A student can take many courses and a course has many students. What is the correct way to store this in a relational database?
options: A `student_ids` column in the `course` table holding comma-separated ids
A separate association table (such as `enrollment`) with both `student_id` and `course_id` as foreign keys
Merging Student and Course into a single table
mad1-w4-q1.explanation: This is a many-to-many (M:N) relationship, and in the relational model it is represented by an association table in which each row is one (student, course) pair. Option A's trap: one column can hold only one course, which makes it 1:N. Option B allows neither a foreign key nor a join, and option D duplicates data again and again.

mad1-w4-q2.question: In a blog app a User can have many Posts, but every Post has exactly one author. Where should the foreign key go?
options: A `user_id` column in the `posts` table, pointing to `users.id`
Each table holding the other's id
A separate association table is required
mad1-w4-q2.explanation: In a 1:N relationship the FK goes on the 'many' side (posts): every post stores the id of its one author. Option A's trap: a user has many posts, so a single `post_id` column cannot hold them all. Option C creates duplicated and inconsistent data, and option D (an association table) is for M:N, which isn't needed here.

mad1-w4-q3.question: `users` has (1, Asha), (2, Bilal), (3, Chen). `posts` has three rows: two with `user_id = 1` and one with `user_id = 3`. What does this query return?
mad1-w4-q3.explanation: The LEFT JOIN keeps Bilal too, with NULL post columns. `COUNT(p.id)` counts only non-NULL values, so Bilal's count is 0. Option B's trap: thinking like `COUNT(*)`, which would count the NULL row as 1. Option C is the INNER JOIN result, and option D is wrong because COUNT never returns NULL; it returns 0.

mad1-w4-q4.question: Which statement about the model below is correct? (The `User` model's table is `user`.)
options: `author` creates a separate column in the database that stores the user's name
`db.ForeignKey('user.id')` is wrong; it should use the class name `'User.id'`
A Post can be saved without a user, because relationships are optional
In the table the link is only the `user_id` column; `post.author` gives the User object and `user.posts` gives that user's list of posts
mad1-w4-q4.explanation: `relationship` creates no column; it provides Python attributes based on the `user_id` FK, and `backref='posts'` adds the reverse attribute on User. Option A's trap: taking the relationship for a column. Option B is wrong because `ForeignKey` takes a table.column name; the class name belongs in `relationship('User')`. Option C is wrong because `user_id` has `nullable=False`.

mad1-w4-q5.question: A Flask-SQLAlchemy view creates `u = User(email='a@x.in')`, calls `db.session.add(u)`, and returns a response without calling `commit()`. What happens?
options: The row is saved automatically at the end of the request
The row is not saved; at the end of the request the session is removed and the uncommitted work is discarded
The row is saved but appears only after the app restarts
`add()` itself raises an error, because add is not allowed without commit
mad1-w4-q5.explanation: `add()` only marks the object as pending in the session; making it permanent in the database is `commit()`'s job. Flask-SQLAlchemy removes the session at the end of the app context, and a transaction that was never committed is rolled back. Option A's trap: assuming an 'auto-save', which is not the default behaviour. Option D is wrong because calling commit after add is the normal flow; add on its own raises no error.

mad1-w4-q6.question: `User.posts` is a relationship that uses the default (lazy) loading. The database has 50 users. How many SELECT queries does this code run in total?
mad1-w4-q6.explanation: The first query loads all 50 users. With lazy loading, every `u.posts` runs a separate SELECT for that user the first time it is accessed, so 50 more queries: 1 + 50 = 51. This is the **N+1 problem**. Option B's trap: that is the count for eager loading such as `selectinload`, not for the default. Option A assumes a single JOIN like `joinedload`, and option C forgets the first query for the users.

mad1-w5-q1.question: A route is defined with `@app.route('/submit')` (no `methods` argument). An HTML form sends `POST /submit`. What is the status of the response?
mad1-w5-q1.explanation: Without `methods`, a route accepts only GET (plus the automatic HEAD/OPTIONS). The URL matches but the method doesn't, so 405. Option B's trap: thinking 'the request failed, so 404'; 404 is for when no rule matches at all. Option A is wrong because the route existing isn't enough, the method must be allowed too, and option D would happen if an exception occurred inside the view.

mad1-w5-q2.question: `<form action="/signup" method="post">` contains `<input name="email">`. Where does the Flask view find this field's value?
mad1-w5-q2.explanation: A POST form's data is form-encoded in the request body, and Flask exposes it as `request.form`. Option B's trap: `request.args` is only the URL's query string, which a GET form fills. Option C is for a JSON body (for example `fetch` sending `application/json`), and option D is for cookies; a normal form submit puts nothing there.

mad1-w5-q3.question: The route is `@app.route('/user/<int:uid>')` and the view is `def profile(uid):`. What happens for the requests `GET /user/42` and `GET /user/abc`?
options: The view runs for both; in the second case `uid` is the string `'abc'`
`/user/42` works; for `/user/abc`, `int()` fails inside the view and a 500 is returned
For `/user/42`, `uid` is the integer 42; `/user/abc` does not match the route at all, so 404
mad1-w5-q3.explanation: The `int` converter checks during matching: if the segment is digits it passes an int to the view, otherwise the rule doesn't match and, with no other rule, the result is 404. Option C's trap: thinking the conversion happens inside the view and a failure crashes it (500); the view never runs. Option B is wrong because the converter changes the type, and option A ignores the converter.

mad1-w5-q4.question: A POST handler that places an order returns `redirect(url_for('order_status', oid=o.id))` on success instead of `render_template('done.html')`. What is the main benefit?
options: Less server load, because a redirect response is small
If the user refreshes, the browser repeats only a GET, not the form's POST, so no duplicate order is created
HTTP does not allow HTML in the response to a POST
The redirect puts the form data into the URL, which helps debugging
mad1-w5-q4.explanation: This is the Post/Redirect/Get pattern: after the redirect the last request in the browser's history is a GET, so a refresh or back/forward does not POST the order again. Option A's trap: seeing the redirect as an optimisation; it actually costs an extra request. Option C is wrong, a POST response can be HTML; the risk is only a resubmit on refresh. Option D is also wrong, the form data does not go into the redirect URL.

mad1-w5-q5.question: The route `@app.route('/post/<int:post_id>')` has the view function `show_post`. Inside a request, what does `url_for('show_post', post_id=7, ref='mail')` return?
options: An error, because `ref` is not in the route
mad1-w5-q5.explanation: `url_for` fills the rule's variables (`post_id`) into the path, and turns any extra arguments that are not in the rule (`ref`) into the query string. Option B's trap: treating an extra argument as an error; Flask quietly puts it in the query. Option D puts every value in the query and option A puts them in the path; both ignore the rule.

mad1-w5-q6.question: A controller validates a form with this function. What is the output of the code?
mad1-w5-q6.explanation: In the first form `'  '.strip()` is an empty string, so there is a `name` error. `'-5'.isdigit()` is False (the minus sign is not a digit), so `age` = 'number'. In the second form `'075'.isdigit()` is True and `int('075')` = 75, which is outside 18–60, so only `age` = 'range'. Option C's trap: treating '-5' as a number and reaching the range check. Option D treats the leading zero as invalid, and option B ignores `strip()`.

mad1-w6-q1.question: According to HTTP semantics, which of these methods is **not idempotent**?
mad1-w6-q1.explanation: POST usually creates a new item in a collection; send the same request twice and you can get two items, so POST is not idempotent. Option B's trap: PUT also changes data, but PUT sets the whole resource to a given state, so after ten calls the final state is the same. GET (option A) is safe and DELETE (option C) is idempotent: deleting again after a delete changes the state no further.

mad1-w6-q2.question: `POST /api/v1/courses` successfully created a new course. Which status code is the most appropriate for the response?
options: 201 Created, with the new course's URI in the `Location` header
mad1-w6-q2.explanation: 201 Created is the standard when a new resource is created, and the `Location` header tells the client where the new resource lives. Option A's trap: 200 also means 'success', so people send it, but it doesn't signal creation. Option D (202) is for work that has been queued and will happen later, and option C is for a success with no body.

mad1-w6-q3.question: An API needs to read all enrollments of student 17. Which of these endpoints is the most RESTful?
mad1-w6-q3.explanation: Enrollments are a sub-resource of the student, the URI has only nouns, and reading uses GET. Option C's trap: the right URI with the wrong method; POST would create a new enrollment in that collection. Options B and D put a verb ('get', 'fetch') in the URI, which is RPC style; in REST the HTTP method does the verb's job.

mad1-w6-q4.question: A client sends `DELETE /api/v1/items/5` and gets 204. Because of a network glitch the client sends the same request again and now gets 404. Is DELETE still called idempotent?
options: No, because the two response codes were different (204 and 404)
Yes, but only if the server sends 204 both times; sending 404 violates the standard
Yes; idempotence is about the effect on server state, and after both cases item 5 is deleted. The response code may differ
No, DELETE is never idempotent; only GET is
mad1-w6-q4.explanation: Idempotent means the request's effect on server state is the same whether it is sent once or many times. After the first DELETE the item is gone, and after the second the state is unchanged, so DELETE is idempotent. Option A's trap: reading idempotence as 'the same response every time'. Option B is wrong because a 404 the second time is perfectly valid, and option D contradicts DELETE's standard property.

mad1-w6-q5.question: An API view sends this payload as JSON. What is the output of the code?
mad1-w6-q5.explanation: `json.dumps` writes keys in double quotes and turns `True` into JSON's `true` and `None` into `null`; the float 99.5 stays as it is. Option A's trap: that is Python's `print` (repr) of a dict, not JSON; single quotes are not valid JSON. Option B turns booleans/None into strings, and option C writes JavaScript's `undefined`, which isn't a JSON type at all.

mad1-w6-q6.question: In a notes API, note 9 belongs to Meera. Three requests: (i) `DELETE /api/notes/9` with no token; (ii) the same request with Ravi's valid token; (iii) `PUT /api/notes/9` with Meera's valid token and the body `{"title": "x"` (closing brace missing, i.e. invalid JSON). In order, what are the most standard status codes?
mad1-w6-q6.explanation: (i) The client gave no identity at all, so 401 Unauthorized (i.e. unauthenticated). (ii) Ravi is identified but the note isn't his, so 403 Forbidden. (iii) The body can't even be parsed, which is the client's fault: 400 Bad Request. Option A's trap: swapping the meanings of 401 and 403. Some APIs deliberately return 404 in (ii) to hide that the note exists, but option C gives 500 for (iii), which is wrong because bad input is not a server error. Option D swaps (i) and (iii).

mad1-w7-q1.question: Where and how does Flask's default `session` (no extensions) keep its data?
options: In the server's memory; the browser only gets a random session id
In a sessions table in the database
In a browser cookie, signed with `SECRET_KEY` but not encrypted; the user can read the content but cannot change it
In a browser cookie, encrypted; the user cannot even read the content
mad1-w7-q1.explanation: Flask's default session is client-side: the data is serialized into a cookie and signed with `SECRET_KEY`, so a modified cookie is rejected, but the content can be read by decoding it. Option D's trap: confusing 'signed' with 'encrypted'. Options A and B describe server-side sessions, which come from extensions such as Flask-Session, not from the default.

mad1-w7-q2.question: To protect a session cookie from being stolen through XSS, i.e. so that page JavaScript cannot read it via `document.cookie`, which cookie attribute do you set?
mad1-w7-q2.explanation: The browser sends an `HttpOnly` cookie with HTTP requests but hides it from JavaScript, so an injected script cannot steal it. Option A's trap: `Secure` is also a security attribute, but it only ensures the cookie travels over HTTPS; JS can still read it. Option C is about cross-site requests (CSRF), and option D expires (deletes) the cookie immediately.

mad1-w7-q3.question: A WSGI app is called with `environ = {'name': 'Zoë'}`. What is the value of the `Content-Length` header?
mad1-w7-q3.explanation: `'Hi Zoë!'` has 7 characters, but in UTF-8 'ë' takes 2 bytes, so the encoded body is 8 bytes, and `len(body)` counts bytes. `Content-Length` is always in bytes, so this is the correct approach. Option B's trap: counting the string's characters (`len` before encoding). Option C counts the characters of the template `Hi {name}!`, and option D takes 'ë' as 3 bytes.

mad1-w7-q4.question: The response to `GET /logo.png` had `Cache-Control: max-age=600` and `ETag: "v7"`. The user loads the same image again 5 minutes later and then 15 minutes after the first request. The image has not changed on the server. What does the browser do?
options: Downloads the full image from the server both times
Uses the cache both times without contacting the server, because an ETag is present
Sends `If-None-Match` at 5 minutes; downloads the full image at 15 minutes
At 5 minutes uses the cache directly (no server contact); at 15 minutes sends a conditional request with `If-None-Match: "v7"`, and the server replies 304 Not Modified
mad1-w7-q4.explanation: max-age=600 means the copy is fresh for 10 minutes, so at 5 minutes the cache is used without any network. At 15 minutes the copy is stale, but there is an ETag, so the browser asks with `If-None-Match`; the image hasn't changed, so the server sends 304 with no body and the cached copy is reused. Option B's trap: treating the ETag as freshness; an ETag is only for revalidation. Option C reverses freshness and revalidation.

mad1-w7-q5.question: An API uses cache-aside. The cache hit ratio is 0.8. A cache check takes 2 ms; on a miss, after the cache check, the DB query takes another 50 ms. What is the average response time (data fetch only)?
mad1-w7-q5.explanation: Hit: 2 ms. Miss: 2 + 50 = 52 ms (first the cache check, then the DB). Average = 0.8 × 2 + 0.2 × 52 = 1.6 + 10.4 = 12 ms. Option A's trap: forgetting the 2 ms cache check on a miss (0.8 × 2 + 0.2 × 50). Option C swaps the hit and miss probabilities, and option D just takes (2 + 50) ÷ 2, as if both happened equally often.

mad1-w7-q6.question: This Flask app has just started on Gunicorn with 2 sync worker **processes**. Assume requests alternate between the two workers (1st to worker A, 2nd to worker B, 3rd to worker A, ...). After 6 requests to `/hits`, what does the 6th response show?
options: An error, because two processes are changing the same `global` variable
mad1-w7-q6.explanation: Each worker process has its own copy of the module, so `hits` is two separate counters. Worker A handled requests 1, 3, 5 and worker B handled 2, 4, 6; the 6th request is worker B's third, so `hits=3`. Option A's trap: assuming all workers share one memory. Option D is wrong because the processes have separate memory, so there is no conflict at all; that is exactly why a shared counter needs a DB or Redis.

mad1-w8-q1.question: For a comment form, what does **progressive enhancement** correctly mean?
options: Build the whole app in a JavaScript framework and show 'Please enable JavaScript' when JS is off
The form works with a normal POST without JavaScript; when JS is available, enhance the same form with `fetch` so the page doesn't reload

mad1-w2-q12.question: `.a` and `.b` are both block children inside `.wrap`. What is the visible width (border to border) of each, and how wide is the content of `.b`?

Option C's trap: subtracting padding and border from one side only (240 − 10 − 2 = 228). Option A applies border-box to `.a` as well, and option B ignores the `box-sizing` of `.b`.

mad1-w2-q13.question: What is the final color of the "Buy" link?
mad1-w2-q13.explanation: Specificity: `.card .btn` = (0, 2, 0), `div a.primary` = (0, 1, 2), `.btn.primary` = (0, 2, 0), `a` = (0, 0, 1). Option B's trap: seeing "more selectors" in (0, 1, 2), when its middle value is 1, lower than 2. Option D is the least specific.

mad1-w2-q14.question: What is the font-size of `.card` at viewport widths of 500px, 600px and 1200px?
mad1-w2-q14.explanation: At 500px no query matches: 14px. At 600px, `min-width: 600px` matches (the boundary is included): 16px. At 1200px both queries match; specificity is equal, so the rule **later** in the source (the 600px query, 16px) wins. Option C's trap: thinking the larger breakpoint wins automatically; here the 1000px query is written first, so it loses. Option A excludes the `min-width` boundary, and option D applies a query at 500px too.

mad1-w2-q15.question: The user clicks Apply without changing anything. Which URL will the browser request?

A checkbox is submitted only when checked, and several checked boxes with the same `name` become separate pairs: `color=red&color=green`. The last input has only an `id`, no `name`, so it is not submitted. Option B's trap: thinking only the last value for a name survives. Option C sends the unchecked box too, and option D treats `id` as if it were `name`.

mad1-w3-q7.question: You want to write a note in a Jinja2 template that is meant for developers and must not appear at all in the HTML sent to the browser. Which syntax do you use?

Option C's trap: to the template engine an HTML comment is ordinary text, so it ends up in the page source where anyone can read it with view-source. Option A prints a value, and option B is for statements (`note` is not a valid tag, so it errors).

mad1-w3-q8.question: The context has `tags = ['flask', 'jinja', 'sql']`. What does `{{ tags|join(', ') }}` render?
mad1-w3-q8.explanation: `join` joins the list items with the given string (here a comma and a space): `flask, jinja, sql`. Option A's trap: that is the Python list representation you get with `{{ tags }}` and no filter. Option C forgets the space in the separator, and option D is like a `join` with no separator.

mad1-w3-q9.question: The controller passes `courses=[]` (an empty list). What appears inside the list?
options: A template error, since a loop cannot run over an empty list
mad1-w3-q9.explanation: The `else` block of a Jinja `for` loop runs when the sequence is empty (the loop runs zero times). So the "No courses" `<li>` appears. Option B's trap: thinking of Python's `for ... else`, where `else` means something different; in Jinja it is for "empty list". Options C and D: on an empty list the loop just runs zero times, with no error and no "None".

mad1-w3-q10.question: The context has `scores = [70, 85, 90]` and `avg = 81.6666`. What does `{{ scores|length }} {{ avg|round(1) }}` render?
mad1-w3-q10.explanation: `length` counts the items: 3. `round(1)` does normal rounding to one decimal: 81.6666 → 81.7 (the next digit is 6, so it rounds up). Option A's trap: treating round as truncation (just cutting digits off). Option B mistakes the length for the last index (2), and option D ignores the argument of `round(1)` and rounds to a whole number.

mad1-w3-q11.question: What does this template render? (The macro definition itself outputs nothing.)
options: An error, because the first call does not pass `kind`
mad1-w3-q11.explanation: A macro works like a function and can take default arguments. The first call does not pass `kind`, so the default `info` applies; the second call passes `warn`. Option A's trap: forgetting the default and treating `kind` as empty. Option B ignores the second call's argument, and option C thinks the argument is required despite the default.

mad1-w3-q12.question: When `page.html` is rendered, what ends up in the title and the body?
mad1-w3-q12.explanation:

Base

`, then `

mad1-w3-q13.question: The context has `students = ['Asha', 'Bilal', 'Chen', 'Dev']`. What does this template (a single line) render?
mad1-w3-q13.explanation: `for ... if` filters the list first: Asha, Chen, Dev. The `loop` variables run over these filtered items only: `loop.first` is true for Asha, giving `[`; after Asha and Chen comes `, `; `loop.last` is true for Dev, giving `]`. Result `[Asha, Chen, Dev]`. Option A's trap: thinking `loop.last` follows the original list, so Dev is not "last". mad1-w3-q14.question: A Flask `.html` template (autoescape on) gets this context: `bio = 'hi'` (written by a user), `tags = ['a', 'b']`, and `ad_html = 'Sale'` (the app's own trusted HTML). What appears in the page's HTML source (view-source)?
mad1-w3-q14.explanation: Autoescape is on, so the `<` and `>` in `{{ bio }}` become entities: `<i>hi</i>`. `join('+')` gives `a+b`. `|safe` turns escaping off, so `Sale` goes out unchanged. Option A's trap: forgetting autoescape (that would be the road to XSS). Option B ignores the effect of `|safe`, and option D swaps the two.

mad1-w3-q15.question: The context has `a = 0`, `c = ''` and `d = 'x'`; `b` is not passed at all. What is the output?
mad1-w3-q15.explanation: Without `true`, `default` applies only to undefined values: `a = 0` is defined, so `0`; `b` is undefined, so `N/A`. With `true`, `default` also applies to falsy values (empty string, 0): `c = ''` → `N/A`, but `d = 'x'` is truthy, so `x`. Option A's trap: treating 0 as "missing", though `a` has no `true`. Option B ignores the `true` argument on `c`, and option C replaces the real value of `d` too.

mad1-w4-q7.question: What is the main job of a **primary key** in a relational table?
options: To point at a row in another table
To keep the table's rows in alphabetical order
mad1-w4-q7.explanation: The primary key is each row's unique identity: no two rows can share a PK, and it is what foreign keys in other tables point at. Option B's trap: that is the foreign key's job, pointing at another table's PK. Option C (ordering) and option D (encryption) are not what a PK does.

mad1-w4-q8.question: Each User has at most one Profile, and each Profile belongs to exactly one User (1:1). What is the best way to model this?
options: A `user_id` FK in the `profile` table, with no other constraint
A `user_id` FK in the `profile` table, with `UNIQUE` on that column
A column of comma-separated profile ids in the `user` table
mad1-w4-q8.explanation: For 1:1 the FK gets a `UNIQUE` constraint, so one user can never get two profiles. Option A's trap: an FK alone gives 1:N, allowing many profiles per user. Option B is for M:N, and option D can take neither an FK nor a join, so it is wrong in relational design.

mad1-w4-q9.question: A wallet transfer must subtract ₹500 from one account and add it to another. The server crashes after the first step. Which database feature makes sure the half-done work is not kept?
options: An index, which finds rows quickly
A transaction: all of it commits or all of it rolls back
A foreign key constraint, which blocks bad references
An ORM, which gives Python objects instead of SQL
mad1-w4-q9.explanation: A transaction makes several changes one unit: if a crash happens before the commit, the database undoes all of them, so money is neither subtracted nor added. Option C's trap: an FK prevents bad references, not half-finished work. Option A (an index) only speeds up searches, and option D (an ORM) is just a way to write code; atomicity comes from the database's transaction.

mad1-w4-q10.question: The table `enrollment(student_id, course_id, course_title)` stores the course title in every enrollment row. What is the biggest problem with this design?
options: No problem; keeping the title avoids a join, so this is best
`(student_id, course_id)` cannot be made a composite primary key
Counting a course's students is not possible in this design
Changing a title means updating many rows; miss one and the data is inconsistent
mad1-w4-q10.explanation: A course's title is one fact, but here it is repeated in every enrollment row. Changing the title means updating every matching row, and if one is missed the same course shows two titles: an update anomaly. The right design keeps the title in `course` and only `course_id` in enrollment. Option A's trap: saving a join is a small gain, inconsistent data is a big cost. Options B and C are wrong: a composite PK and `COUNT` both still work here.

mad1-w4-q11.question: What does this Flask-SQLAlchemy code print?
mad1-w4-q11.explanation: The first commit saves MAD1. In the second transaction the duplicate MAD1 and DBMS are both pending; the commit hits `IntegrityError` on the duplicate and `rollback()` undoes that **whole** transaction, DBMS included. So only the first MAD1 is left: 1. Option C's trap: thinking DBMS got saved separately; a transaction either happens completely or not at all. Option A ignores the unique constraint, and option D assumes the rollback also undoes the earlier commit.

mad1-w4-q12.question: What does this query return? (each row: code, a, b)
mad1-w4-q12.explanation: The LEFT JOIN keeps Java, with one row whose `e` columns are NULL. `COUNT(*)` counts rows, so Java's `a` = 1; `COUNT(e.student_id)` counts only non-NULL values, so `b` = 0. MAD1's 2 enrollments and DBMS's 1 give the same value in both counts. Option A's trap: thinking `COUNT(*)` also skips the NULL row. Option B is the INNER JOIN result, and option D treats `COUNT(column)` as if it counted NULLs too.

mad1-w4-q13.question: `User.posts` is eager-loaded with `selectinload`, but `Post.comments` is the default lazy. There are 20 users and each has 3 posts. How many SELECT queries run in total?
mad1-w4-q13.explanation: 1 query for the users, 1 query (selectinload) to fetch all 60 posts together. Then `p.comments` is lazy on every post, so 60 separate queries. Total = 1 + 1 + 60 = 62. Option B's trap: that is the count without selectinload (1 + 20 + 60). Option C assumes the eager loading reached the comments too, and option D counts the comment queries per user (20) instead of per post.

mad1-w4-q14.question: A library app: a Member borrows many Books, a Book is borrowed by many Members over time, and each borrow's date must be stored. Each Book has exactly one Publisher, and a Publisher has many Books. Which design is best?
options: 3 tables; `member_id` and `publisher_id` FKs in `book`, with the date in `book` too
4 tables; a `book_id` FK in `publisher`, and `loan(member_id, book_id, borrowed_on)`
5 tables; an association table for publisher–book too, plus a separate `loan` table
4 tables; a `book.publisher_id` FK and `loan(member_id, book_id, borrowed_on)`
mad1-w4-q14.explanation: Member–Book is M:N, and the borrow date is an attribute of the relationship, so an association table `loan` holds both FKs and `borrowed_on`. Publisher–Book is 1:N, so the FK goes on the "many" side: `book.publisher_id`. Total: member, book, publisher, loan = 4. Option A's trap: `book.member_id` can hold only one member, not M:N. Option B puts the FK on the "one" side, and option C adds an association table that 1:N does not need.

mad1-w4-q15.question: After all three steps, how many rows are in the `student` table, and what name is stored for Bilal?
options: 1 row (only Chen); the rollback removed everything
mad1-w4-q15.explanation: Step (1) commits Asha and Bilal. Then the name is changed but not committed; the rollback in step (2) undoes only that uncommitted change, so the name stays `Bilal`. Step (3) commits Chen. Total 3 rows. Option C's trap: thinking the database changes as soon as the object's value changes; nothing is permanent without a commit. Option D assumes a rollback also removes already-committed data, and option A forgets Chen's commit.

mad1-w5-q7.question: The request is `GET /search?q=lamp&page=2`. How do you read the value of `page` in a Flask view?
mad1-w5-q7.explanation: Query string values are in `request.args`. Option A's trap: `request.form` is for the body of a POSTed form, not the URL. Option C is for a JSON body (there is no body here), and option D is for cookies. Note: the value comes back as the string `'2'`; convert it if you need an int.

mad1-w5-q8.question: A view does `return redirect(url_for('home'))` with no `code` argument. What is the response's status code?
mad1-w5-q8.explanation: Flask's `redirect()` sends 302 (temporary redirect) by default, with a `Location` header. Option B's trap: 301 is the permanent redirect, which you only get by passing `code=301`. Option A would be for rendering the page directly, and option D has nothing to do with redirects.

mad1-w5-q9.question: The signup form's input has HTML `required` and `maxlength="20"`. Why is server-side validation still needed?
options: Browser checks are easily bypassed with curl, devtools or a script
Server validation makes the page load faster
Flask reads the HTML attributes and validates by itself, so nothing extra is needed
mad1-w5-q9.explanation: Anyone can send a request without a browser (curl, a script) or strip the attributes in devtools, so every input must be checked on the server. Option B's trap: `required` works in all modern browsers; the problem is bypassing. Option C has nothing to do with validation, and option D is wrong: Flask never even looks at HTML attributes.

mad1-w5-q10.question: Two POST requests arrive: the first has body `name=Asha` (no phone), the second has body `phone=999` (no name). What status does each get?
mad1-w5-q10.explanation: `request.form.get('phone', '')` returns the default when the key is missing, so the first request gets 200 with `ok Asha`. The second is missing `name`, and when `request.form['name']` cannot find the key, Flask sends 400 Bad Request by itself. Option B's trap: treating the missing `phone` as an error, though `.get()` is used for it. Option A assumes a missing key just gives an empty value, and option C treats both the same.

mad1-w5-q11.question: Two apps differ in one route: App 1 has `@app.route('/files/<fp>')`, App 2 has `@app.route('/files/<path:fp>')`. Both receive `GET /files/docs/a.txt`. What happens?
mad1-w5-q11.explanation: The default `string` converter takes text without slashes, so `docs/a.txt` (which has a slash) does not match App 1's rule: 404. The `path` converter accepts slashes too, so App 2 gets the whole `docs/a.txt`. Option D's trap: thinking the string converter takes the first part and drops the rest; a rule matches the whole URL or not at all. Option A treats the two converters the same.

mad1-w5-q12.question: An order form's POST handler exists in two versions. Version P (PRG): on success, `redirect(url_for('order', oid=o.id))`. Version R: on success, a direct `render_template('done.html')`. In each, the user submits one order, then presses refresh 2 times on the result page (confirming resubmission when the browser asks). How many orders does each version create in total?
mad1-w5-q12.explanation: In P, after the POST the browser does a GET to `/order/...`, so a refresh repeats only that GET: 1 order. In R the result page is itself the POST's response, so every refresh sends the same POST again: 1 + 2 = 3 orders. PRG exists to avoid exactly this duplication. Option D's trap: not counting the first submit. Option B assumes a refresh never repeats a POST, and option C ignores PRG's redirect.

mad1-w5-q13.question: This server-side validation function is run on three inputs. What is the output?

Second: `'-5'.isdigit()` is False (a minus sign is not a digit), so `roll`, and the `range` check never runs (`elif`); the email has no `@`, so `email`. Third: roll is missing, the default `''` is not digits, so `roll`. Option A's trap: treating -5 as a number and giving a range error. Option C lets the missing field pass, and option D treats 61 as in range (misreading the boundary).

mad1-w5-q14.question: Four requests arrive: (i) `DELETE /items`, (ii) `GET /items/x7`, (iii) `POST /items/5`, (iv) `HEAD /items/5`. Which status codes does Flask return?
mad1-w5-q14.explanation: (i) The `/items` rule matches but DELETE is not allowed: 405. (ii) `x7` is not an int, so `<int:iid>` does not match at all: 404. (iii) The rule matches, but no `methods` were given, so only GET is allowed: 405. (iv) When GET is allowed, Flask handles HEAD by itself: 200 (with no body). Option A's trap: treating HEAD as "not allowed" too. Option B calls the wrong method in (i) a 404, and option C treats a converter mismatch as 400.

mad1-w5-q15.question: The business rule lives in a service function that raises an exception (the controller will later turn it into a flash message or status). What is the output?

Second `bilal` call: already in the list → False (it never reaches the capacity check). `chen`: the size is now 2 ≥ cap 2, so `CourseFull` is raised, the `'ok'` line is skipped and `except` appends `'full'`. There are still 2 students. Option B's trap: forgetting the capacity check. Options A and D ignore the duplicate check (adding bilal twice).

mad1-w6-q7.question: Which of these HTTP methods is **safe**, meaning it does not change server state?
mad1-w6-q7.explanation: GET (and HEAD) are safe: they only read and change nothing. The trap in options B and C: PUT and DELETE are **idempotent** (repeating them has the same effect), but not safe, since the first call does change state. Option A (POST) is neither safe nor idempotent.

mad1-w6-q8.question: Which request is the most RESTful way to delete course 12?
mad1-w6-q8.explanation: In REST the URI names the resource (a noun) and the method names the action (a verb): `DELETE` on `/courses/12`. Option B's trap: changing data with GET is dangerous, since crawlers and prefetch run GETs assuming they are safe, and a verb in the URI is RPC style. Options C and D also put a verb into the URI.

mad1-w6-q9.question: A Flask view returns the dict `{'deleted_at': None}`. How does `None` appear in the JSON response?
mad1-w6-q9.explanation: Python's `None` becomes `null` in JSON (and `True` → `true`). Option A's trap: assuming the Python name carries over to JSON; JSON has its own type system. Option B is the name used by some other languages, and option D is a JavaScript value that does not exist in the JSON format.

mad1-w6-q10.question: A mobile app sends `GET /api/v1/orders` with an `Authorization: Bearer ...` header, but the token expired yesterday. Which status should the API return?
mad1-w6-q10.explanation: An expired token means the client's identity is not valid: "first tell me who you are", which is 401. The client can get a new token and retry. Option A's trap: 403 is for a valid identity without permission. Option C is for a resource that is not found, and option D for a malformed request; the request's format is fine here.

mad1-w6-q11.question: Cart item 3 has `qty` 2. Case 1: the client sends `PATCH /api/cart/3` with body `{"op": "increment", "by": 1}` three times. Case 2 (starting again from qty 2): the client sends `PUT /api/cart/3` with body `{"qty": 4}` three times. What is `qty` at the end of each case?
options: 5 in case 1, 4 in case 2; PUT is idempotent, this PATCH is not
3 in case 1, 12 in case 2; both are non-idempotent
4 in both cases; PUT and PATCH are both idempotent
5 in case 1, 12 in case 2; both add to the value every time
mad1-w6-q11.explanation: Increment adds 1 each time: 2 → 3 → 4 → 5. PUT replaces the whole value, so whether sent three times or once, qty stays 4. That is why PUT is idempotent and an "add" PATCH like this is not. Option B's trap: counting the increment only once and adding up the PUTs (3 × 4). Option C treats the PATCH as idempotent too, and option D reads PUT as "add 4 each time".

mad1-w6-q12.question: The database has 47 courses (ids 1 to 47, in id order). API pagination starts at 1, and `limit` is the number of items per page. Which ids does `GET /api/v1/courses?page=3&limit=20` return, and how many pages are there in total?
options: No items (0 items); 2 pages in total

Option A's trap: forgetting the total and assuming a full 20 items. Option B counts pages from 0 (taking an offset of 1 × 20 instead of 2 × 20), and option D rounds 47 ÷ 20 down to 2 pages, so it thinks page 3 is empty.

mad1-w6-q13.question: Simplified logic of a create-course API (it only returns the status code). What is the output?

Option A's trap: forgetting that the first call stored DBMS. Option B creates a course even with `code` missing, and option C accepts a list body as valid.

mad1-w6-q14.question: What is the **second** printed line of this code?
mad1-w6-q14.explanation: The first line is `{"id": 7, "tags": ["a", "b"], "ok": false, "score": null}`: the tuple becomes a JSON array. Loading it back with `loads` turns the array into a Python **list**, not a tuple. In Python `['a', 'b'] == ('a', 'b')` is False, so `back == data` is False. Option C's trap: thinking a round trip gives back exactly the same data. Options B and D assume JSON remembers the tuple, though JSON has no tuple type at all.

mad1-w6-q15.question: On a client timeout, a library automatically resends every request once (the first request had already reached the server). Which of these can cause an **extra effect** (a duplicate) on the server when repeated? (i) `GET /courses` (ii) `PUT /courses/5` with a full body (iii) `POST /orders` (iv) `DELETE /courses/5` (v) `PATCH /cart/3` with body `{"op": "increment"}`
mad1-w6-q15.explanation: GET is safe; PUT and DELETE are idempotent: repeating them leaves the same final state (a second DELETE may return 404, but the state does not change). POST will create another order, and the increment PATCH will add one more; both are non-idempotent. Option A's trap: thinking PATCH is always idempotent. Option C treats PUT like POST, and option D mistakes DELETE's second response (404) for an "extra effect".

mad1-w7-q7.question: Which cookie attribute makes sure the browser sends the cookie only over HTTPS connections?

mad1-w7-q8.question: The server sends `Set-Cookie: theme=dark; Path=/` (no `Max-Age`, no `Expires`). How long does this cookie last?
options: Forever, until the user deletes it by hand
Until the browser is closed (a session cookie)
Only for the very next single request
Exactly 24 hours, and then it expires
mad1-w7-q8.explanation: Without `Max-Age`/`Expires` it is a "session cookie", removed when the browser closes. Option A's trap: a long life needs `Max-Age` or `Expires`; forever is not the default. Option C is wrong, since the browser keeps sending it with every matching request, and option D is not a default that exists.

mad1-w7-q9.question: Users' order data must never be lost and must be visible to every app server. Where do you keep it?
options: Only in a Redis cache, with no database
mad1-w7-q9.explanation: A database is durable, shared by all processes and transactional: the right place for important data. Option C's trap: a cache is fast and shared, but data can be evicted at any time, so keep only "can be rebuilt" data there. Option B is separate per worker and lost on restart, and option D lives in the user's browser (up to 4 KB).

mad1-w7-q10.question: Flask's default session holds `{'user_id': 5}`. A user copies the cookie, decodes it, changes `user_id` to 1, builds a new cookie and sends it. What happens?
options: The cookie cannot be decoded at all, since Flask session data is encrypted
The server treats them as user 1, since the signed cookie says so
The server crashes on the signature error and returns 500 Internal Server Error
The user can read it, but the signature will not match, so the session is rejected

But changing a value breaks the signature, and Flask rejects that cookie and treats the session as empty. Option B's trap: thinking the server trusts whatever the cookie says; the signature exists to stop exactly that. Option C: an invalid signature is a normal case, not a crash.

mad1-w7-q11.question: The response to `GET /app.css` had `Cache-Control: max-age=60` and `ETag: "a1"`. 2 minutes later the user reloads the page, and meanwhile the file has changed on the server (new ETag `"a2"`). What happens?
options: The browser keeps using the old cached file without asking the server
The browser sends `If-None-Match: "a1"`; the file changed, so 200 + new content and `ETag: "a2"`
The browser sends `If-None-Match: "a1"`, and the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body
The browser sends `If-None-Match: "a2"`, and the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body

mad1-w7-q12.question: This WSGI app handles two requests: `GET /greet?name=ravi` and `GET /greet/`. What are the status and `Content-Length` of each?

mad1-w7-q13.question: An API uses cache-aside. A cache check takes 1 ms; on a miss, the DB takes another 40 ms after the check. The hit ratio drops from 0.9 to 0.6. What is the average data-fetch time before and after?

mad1-w7-q14.question: The app runs on Gunicorn with 2 worker processes (A, B), and requests alternate: request 1 → A, 2 → B, 3 → A. In request 1 Asha logs in; in requests 2 and 3 she opens `/home` (the cookie is sent). What does she get on requests 2 and 3?

mad1-w7-q15.question: Behind a load balancer are 3 stateless app servers, each handling at most 200 req/s. Every request makes one DB query, and the database handles at most 300 queries/s. mad1-w8-q7.question: A page has 5 elements with class `.item`. What does `document.querySelector('.item')` return?

mad1-w8-q8.question: The `<head>` contains `<script src="app.js" defer></script>`. What does `defer` do?

mad1-w8-q9.question: You need to POST a JSON object `data` to the server with `fetch`. Which options object is right?

mad1-w8-q10.question: The user clicks the "Delete" button. What appears in the console?

The event bubbles up to the `ul` listener, and `closest('li')` walks up from the button to the first `li`: `item-7`. This is event delegation. mad1-w8-q11.question: A name arrives from an API: `name = ''`. Code A: `el.innerHTML = name`. Code B: `el.textContent = name`. What happens in each?
options: Both show the whole string as plain text only

mad1-w8-q12.question: In what order does this code print?

mad1-w8-q13.question: The network is fine, and the server answers `/api/users/9` with status 404 and body `{"error": "no user"}`. What appears in the console?

mad1-w8-q14.question: Every student gets 5 grace marks; 50 or above is a pass, those at 90 or above get 2 points, and other passing students 1 point. What does the code print?

mad1-w9-q7.question: The site runs over HTTPS. Which of these does HTTPS **not** provide?

Protection from the app's XSS or SQL injection bugs

But bugs inside the app (XSS, SQL injection, wrong authorization) work just the same inside an encrypted channel. Trap: assuming "HTTPS = secure app"; HTTPS only secures the transport.

mad1-w9-q8.question: On the login form, the server checks the email and password and confirms that the person sending the request is Kabir. What is this step called?
mad1-w9-q8.explanation: Authentication answers "who are you?", and confirming identity by checking a password is exactly that. Option A's trap: authorization is the next step, "is Kabir allowed to do this?". Option C is about hiding data, and option D is a database design concept.

mad1-w9-q9.question: A search feature uses the user's input in an SQL query. What is the best way to prevent SQL injection?
options: Stripping single quotes from the input is enough
Changing the search form from GET to POST
Using a parameterized query (`?` placeholder) or an ORM
mad1-w9-q9.explanation: In a parameterized query the value travels separately from the query's structure, so however odd the input is, it stays data and never becomes SQL. Option A's trap: stripping quotes is incomplete (numbers, comments and encoding tricks get through) and it breaks real names like O'Brien. Options B and D have nothing to do with injection: a POST body is just as controllable, and HTTPS only secures the transport.

mad1-w9-q10.question: Riya and Sameer both use the password `sunflower9`. The app takes a random salt per user and stores a PBKDF2 hash. What is the biggest benefit of the salt?
options: Their hashes differ, and precomputed (rainbow) tables become useless
The salt makes the hash reversible, so forgotten passwords can be recovered
The salt makes hashing faster, so login is quicker
The salt must be kept secret; if it leaks the hash breaks at once

Option B is wrong: the hash stays one-way. Option C's trap: it is slowness (iterations), not speed, that makes brute force costly. Option D: the salt is stored next to the hash and is not secret; its job is uniqueness.

mad1-w9-q11.question: An attacker's site has a hidden form that auto-submits `POST https://bank.test/transfer` as soon as the page opens. A logged-in victim visits that site and their session cookie goes along with the request. Which defence stops this attack?

A random CSRF token in every form, checked against the server session
Hashing every password with bcrypt and a salt
Serving the whole bank site over HTTPS only, with HSTS

Option A's trap: the endpoint is already POST and the attacker's form sends a POST too. Option C is about password storage, and option D: over HTTPS the browser still sends the cookie automatically.

mad1-w9-q12.question: In a vulnerable login, an attacker types `x' OR name = 'chen` into the pin field. Which rows does the query return?

Option C assumes a correct username will come back, and option A ignores the injection's effect entirely.

mad1-w9-q13.question: The login check is run on three attempts. What is the output?

Option D ignores case, and option A ignores the space too. `compare_digest` compares in constant time so timing leaks nothing.

mad1-w9-q14.question: Three bugs: (i) a comment is saved in the DB and shown to everyone with `{{ c.text|safe }}`; (ii) a search page shows the URL's `q` parameter directly with `You searched: {{ q|safe }}`; (iii) JS does `el.innerHTML = location.hash.slice(1)`. Which XSS type is each bug?

mad1-w9-q15.question: Ravi is logged in and sends `POST /notes/9/delete` with the correct CSRF token from his own session. Note 9 belongs to Meera. What happens, and what is the right fix?

mad1-w10-q7.question: By the test pyramid, which tests should a healthy project have the most of?

mad1-w10-q8.question: In a test, after `client = app.test_client()`, you run `client.get('/')`. What happens inside?

mad1-w10-q11.question: A test must run `checkout()` without the real gateway. Which patch target puts a fake `charge` inside `checkout()`?

mad1-w10-q13.question: These are the only two tests and both pass. Which statement about coverage is right?
options: Line coverage is 100%, but branch coverage is only 50%

mad1-w10-q14.question: `time.time` is patched to make the time deterministic. What is the output?

mad1-w10-q15.question: This file is run with `pytest` (tests run in file order). Then only `pytest -k again` is run. What are the results each time?

`test_add` fails, `test_add_again` passes; it passes alone too

mad1-w11-q7.question: How long does data stored in `sessionStorage` last?

mad1-w11-q8.question: In a PWA, what is the job of the **Web App Manifest** file?

Catching network requests and serving offline responses from the Cache API
Sending and scheduling push notifications to users from the server
Keeping the site's HTTPS certificate and private key safe

mad1-w11-q9.question: By WCAG AA, what is the minimum contrast ratio between normal-size text and its background?

mad1-w11-q11.question: A site's menu is built like this: `Pricing`. Clicking works fine for users. What is the biggest SEO problem?

The `onclick` handler slows the page down a lot
The pricing page's `<title>` and meta description are wrong
Crawlers follow only `<a href>` links, not the span

mad1-w11-q12.question: A service worker lives at `/app/sw.js`, and `navigator.serviceWorker.register('/app/sw.js')` (no `scope` option) is called from the `/app/start` page. Which of these pages will the worker control: `/app/`, `/app/reports/q3`, `/apps`, `/help`?

mad1-w11-q13.question: These names are tried with `customElements.define(name, SomeClass)`: `user-card`, `UserCard`, `my-Button`, `x-1`, `card`. Which names are valid?

mad1-w11-q15.question: The service worker is active and the user goes offline. They make three requests: `/static/app.css`, `/courses` and `/`. What happens?

`/static/app.css` and `/` come from the cache; the fetch for `/courses` fails

mad1-w12-q7.question: In Docker, what is the right difference between an **image** and a **container**?

A container is a read-only package; an image is its running instance

mad1-w12-q9.question: A team has development, staging and production environments. What is the main purpose of **staging**?
options: Writing and debugging new code on a developer's laptop
A production-like setup to check a release without real users
A separate place only for running unit tests in CI
A place to keep daily backups of the production database

mad1-w12-q10.question: An endpoint must handle 120 req/s. Each request keeps a sync worker busy for 250 ms on average, and each sync worker handles one request at a time. What is the minimum number of workers needed?

mad1-w12-q11.question: The app sits behind an Nginx reverse proxy, and the logs show client IP `127.0.0.1` for every request. How can the app learn the user's real IP?

From the `Host` header the browser sends
From the `User-Agent` header the browser sends

mad1-w12-q12.question: The latencies (ms) of 20 requests to an endpoint: 22, 15, 400, 18, 21, 12, 30, 19, 90, 25, 16, 14, 48, 22, 20, 35, 18, 27, 15, 24. Using the nearest-rank method (p-th percentile = the value at rank ⌈p/100 × n⌉ in the sorted list), what are p50 and p95?

mad1-w12-q15.question: Behind a load balancer are 4 container instances. Each has 1 CPU and runs (2 × cores) + 1 Gunicorn sync workers; each request keeps a worker busy for 60 ms on average. Peak traffic is 160 req/s. During a rolling deploy (one instance out at a time), what is the capacity, and can it handle the traffic?
options: 150 req/s; no, so add an extra instance before deploying or pick a low-traffic time
100 req/s; no, because half the instances are out during a deploy
150 req/s; yes, because the load balancer always queues the extra requests
mad1-w12-q15.explanation: Workers = 2 × 1 + 1 = 3 per instance. One instance = 3 ÷ 0.06 = 50 req/s, so 4 instances = 200 req/s. During a rolling deploy one instance is out: 3 × 50 = 150 req/s, below 160, so it is overloaded. Option A's trap: assuming full capacity during the deploy. Option C reads a rolling deploy as "half the instances out", and option D takes a queue for capacity; a queue only adds latency, not throughput.
